text: What are the ACID properties of a transaction? Give an example of each.
expectedAnswerPoints: Atomicity: a transaction executes fully or not at all, with partial changes rolled back on failure
Consistency: the database moves from one valid state to another, with all constraints satisfied
Isolation: concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other's intermediate state
Durability: once committed, changes survive crashes, typically via write-ahead logging
Example: a bank transfer must debit and credit together (atomicity) and must persist once confirmed (durability)

text: Explain the three levels of data abstraction in a DBMS.
expectedAnswerPoints: Physical level: how data is actually stored on disk, including file structures, blocks and indexes
Logical level: what data is stored and how it relates, in terms of tables, columns, data types and constraints
View level: customised subsets of the logical data presented to particular users
Each higher level is insulated from changes made at the level beneath it
Developers work at the logical level while users see the view level and the physical level stays hidden

text: What is the difference between logical and physical data independence?
expectedAnswerPoints: Logical independence is the ability to change the logical schema without rewriting application programs
Example of logical independence: splitting an Address column into Street, City and PIN without breaking existing apps
Physical independence is the ability to change physical storage without affecting the logical schema
Example of physical independence: moving data from HDD to SSD or adding an index, with no SQL changes needed
Physical independence is easier to achieve in practice than logical independence

text: Explain super key, candidate key, primary key, alternate key and foreign key.
expectedAnswerPoints: A super key is any set of columns that uniquely identifies a row, possibly with redundant columns
A candidate key is a minimal super key: removing any column destroys uniqueness
The primary key is the candidate key chosen as the official row identifier; it must be unique and not null
Alternate keys are the remaining candidate keys not chosen as primary
A foreign key references the primary or alternate key of another table and may be null if the relationship is optional
Every primary key is a candidate key and every candidate key is a super key, but not the reverse

text: What is a functional dependency? Explain partial and transitive dependencies.
expectedAnswerPoints: X determines Y means any two rows agreeing on X must agree on Y
A partial dependency is when a non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite primary key
Partial dependencies violate 2NF and are removed by splitting the table
A transitive dependency is when a non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute, so A determines B and B determines C
Transitive dependencies violate 3NF and cause update anomalies
Example: roll number determines student name is a partial dependency if the key is (roll number, course code)

text: What is BCNF, and how does it differ from 3NF?
expectedAnswerPoints: BCNF requires that for every functional dependency X determines Y, X must be a super key
3NF additionally allows a dependency where the dependent attribute is itself part of a candidate key
BCNF is therefore stricter: every BCNF relation is in 3NF, but not every 3NF relation is in BCNF
BCNF violations typically arise when there are overlapping candidate keys
Decomposing to BCNF is always lossless but may not preserve all functional dependencies
3NF can always be achieved while preserving dependencies, which is why it is sometimes preferred

text: What is denormalisation? When is it justified and what does it cost?
expectedAnswerPoints: Deliberately introducing controlled redundancy to avoid expensive joins
Techniques include merging tables, adding derived/pre-computed columns, and materialised views
Justified for read-heavy, write-light workloads such as dashboards and analytics reports
Costs include extra storage and slower writes because duplicated data must be kept in sync
Main risk is update anomalies and stale data when copies drift out of sync
Should be applied only after measuring that joins are the real bottleneck

text: What is the difference between the WHERE and HAVING clauses in SQL?
expectedAnswerPoints: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping takes place
HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY has been applied
Aggregate functions cannot be used in WHERE but can be used in HAVING
Logical evaluation order is FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT
Filtering early in WHERE is usually more efficient because fewer rows reach the grouping stage

text: Explain INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN.
expectedAnswerPoints: INNER JOIN returns only rows with a match in both tables
LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matching rows from the right, with nulls where there is no match
RIGHT JOIN returns all rows from the right table plus matching rows from the left
FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables, with nulls where there is no match on either side
A LEFT JOIN with a WHERE clause requiring the right key to be null finds rows present only in the left table

text: What are the isolation levels in SQL, and which anomaly does each prevent?
expectedAnswerPoints: Read Uncommitted prevents nothing and allows dirty reads
Read Committed prevents dirty reads by only reading committed data
Repeatable Read additionally prevents non-repeatable reads by holding shared locks on read rows
Serializable additionally prevents phantom reads, typically using range or predicate locks
A dirty read sees another transaction's uncommitted change that may later be rolled back
Stronger isolation means more safety but more locking and lower concurrency

text: Explain dirty read, non-repeatable read and phantom read with examples.
expectedAnswerPoints: Dirty read: a transaction reads data written by another transaction that has not committed and may roll back
Non-repeatable read: a transaction reads the same row twice and gets different values because another transaction updated and committed in between
Phantom read: a transaction re-runs a range query and sees new rows that another transaction inserted and committed
The difference is that non-repeatable reads concern changed rows while phantoms concern newly appearing rows
They are prevented by Read Committed, Repeatable Read and Serializable respectively

text: What is two-phase locking (2PL), and how does strict 2PL improve on it?
expectedAnswerPoints: 2PL has a growing phase where a transaction acquires locks and a shrinking phase where it releases them
Once a transaction releases any lock it may not acquire another
This guarantees conflict serializability
Basic 2PL still permits cascading aborts, because another transaction may read data that is later rolled back
Strict 2PL holds all exclusive locks until commit or abort
Strict 2PL prevents both dirty reads and dirty writes and is what most real systems implement

text: What is an index, and what is the trade-off in adding one?
expectedAnswerPoints: An index is an auxiliary sorted structure that lets the database locate rows without scanning the whole table
It turns a sequential scan into a lookup, typically O(log n) with a B+ tree
The cost is extra storage plus slower inserts, updates and deletes, since every index must be maintained
Indexes are only used if the query allows it; applying a function to an indexed column usually prevents index use
Over-indexing a write-heavy table can do more harm than good

text: What is the difference between a B-tree and a B+ tree, and why do databases prefer B+ trees for indexes?
expectedAnswerPoints: In a B-tree, keys and data pointers appear in both internal nodes and leaves
In a B+ tree, all keys are duplicated down to the leaves and internal nodes only guide the search
B+ tree leaves are linked left to right in a sequential chain
The linked leaves make range scans and ordered traversal very efficient
Because internal nodes hold only keys, each node fits more keys, giving a shallower tree and fewer disk reads
This is why most DBMS index implementations use B+ trees

text: What is sharding, and what makes a good shard key?
expectedAnswerPoints: Sharding splits a large database horizontally into independent pieces called shards, each hosted separately
It is a form of horizontal scaling that improves performance, scalability and availability
Common strategies are range-based, hash-based, directory-based and geographic sharding
A good shard key has high cardinality so data can spread across many shards
It should distribute traffic evenly to avoid hotspots on popular values
Monotonically increasing keys such as timestamps make poor shard keys because all new writes land on one shard
